blog_summary: The blog post discusses a paper from SIGMOD'19 that proposes extending SQL to handle streaming data more effectively. Adrian Colyer highlights the paper's thesis that SQL, with minor non-intrusive extensions, can be a powerful and syntactically idiomatic way to manage both streams and tables. The authors, experts from Apache Beam, Calcite, and Flink, argue that SQL's familiarity and declarative nature reduce development costs compared to non-standardized stream processing APIs. Key insights include the unification of tables and streams under a single relational model using Time-Varying Relations (TVRs), where streams are just time-varying tables. The paper introduces extensions like event timestamps, watermarks, and windowing functions (e.g., Tumble and Hop) to handle event time semantics. The proposed SQL extensions enable efficient stream processing tasks such as windowed aggregations and joins, with practical benefits like reprocessing recorded streams using the same queries as live data. The blog also notes the adoption of these ideas by major companies like Alibaba and Uber.
paper_title: One SQL to rule them all: an efficient and syntactically idiomatic approach to management of streams and tables
paper_abstract: CCS CONCEPTS Real-time data analysis and management are increasingly critical for today’s businesses. SQL is the de facto lingua franca for these endeavors, yet support for robust streaming analysis and management with SQL remains limited. Many approaches restrict semantics to a reduced subset of features and/or require a suite of non-standard constructs. Additionally, use of event timestamps to provide native support for analyzing events according to when they actually occurred is not pervasive, and often comes with important limitations. We present a three-part proposal for integrating robust streaming into the SQL standard, namely: (1) time-varying relations as a foundation for classical tables as well as streaming data, (2) event time semantics, (3) a limited set of optional keyword extensions to control the materialization of timevarying query results. Motivated and illustrated using examples and lessons learned from implementations in Apache Calcite, Apache Flink, and Apache Beam, we show how with these minimal additions it is possible to utilize the complete suite of standard SQL semantics to perform robust stream processing. • Information systems → Stream management; Query languages; Publication rights licensed to ACM.
